#217. Black girls in LA keep seeing women around them getting killed. They’re driving change

Black women and girls represent an outsized share of LA homicide victims – frustrated with police and legislators’ failures, they’re stepping up and speaking out to stop the violence

As a child, Tioni Theus was a ball of energy. After school she liked to play golf and dance. On weekends, she’d go to the movies and the mall with her older cousin. Driving back home at the end of the day to her family’s apartment in South Los Angeles, California, she’d ask: “What are we doing next?”

Everything changed when Tioni was 13. Her mother was hit by a car and critically injured, leaving her unable to take care of her daughter. While her mom recovered, Tioni lived with other family members. But the accident left Tioni angry, her older cousin Nafeesah Kincy said, and she struggled to understand that her life had permanently changed.

Tioni started talking to strangers online, Kincy noticed, and hung out with unfamiliar people, including older teen boys and young men. Then she left her family’s care and would bounce between random people’s houses, Kincy said, or spend nights with a boyfriend at a hotel. Each time she saw Tioni, Kincy would implore her to come back to her family.

Over the next two years, Tioni stopped going to school and became “lost in the streets”, said Kincy, who would take her cousin to get food, or meet at another family member’s house to drop off care packages with deodorant, clean underwear and tampons. Family members pleaded with Tioni to stay with one of them permanently.

“It was devastating because I couldn’t protect her,” she said. “We did everything we knew to do.”

Then, on 8 January 2021, Tioni’s body was found on a stretch of highway with a gunshot wound to her neck. She was 16. How she ended up there remains unknown.

Tioni’s killing shocked many in Los Angeles, but it outraged LA’s Black community. In the weeks following her death, there were repeated calls for a swift investigation, for compassion from local leaders, and tangible measures to curb the violence. Black women and girls make up about four percent of the population in the LA region, but represent an outsized share of female homicide victims.

Local and state leaders said they heard their calls. They put together a $115,000 reward for information, and the city commissioned a report to better understand why Black women are killed more often than women of other races. But five years later, there have not been any arrests for her killing, and families, community organizers and violence prevention workers say not enough has changed to prevent future deaths.

Families and organizers want local governments and police to be more outspoken about the harms Black women and teen girls face, to study the dynamics more deeply, to fund programs that address the intersection of domestic and community violence, and to make gender-based violence a key component of the region’s general violence prevention strategy.

“We are in a climate where Black women are the most unprotected species,” Kincy said. “We’re not looked at as human. Even our own men don’t feel the need to protect, and it’s scary, it’s sad and disheartening.”

At the same time, some of the root causes of this violence, including misogyny and long-held stereotypes about Black women and girls, can’t be legislated or policed away. So Black women in LA are doing it themselves, using taskforces, rallies, summer programs and podcasts to share their stories. Doing this, they say, can grow the number of people who are looking out for them – which is particularly important right now after the Trump administration cut millions in federal funds for gun violence prevention.

“It feels like people just don’t care,” said Ken’Niyia, 15. “It feels like Black women are not seen as something that should be protected.”

Ken’Niyia, a 15-year-old track-and-field athlete who sports two long french braids, lives in Inglewood, one of several Black- and brown-majority cities in LA county. Over the summer, she enrolled in a program that gave teen girls a place to connect with each other, share their experiences and learn about systemic racism, gender-based violence, rape culture, and the myriad ways generations of Black women have overcome them.

The program has given the girls the rare opportunity to talk about their shared experiences of feeling unsafe in their neighborhoods, and understanding the ways stereotypes about Black women and girls influence their lives, they said.

“We talk about things that are important to know when you’re a teen trying to navigate life,” said 17-year-old Laniyah. “It gives us Black girls a chance to be vulnerable with each other.”

The girls say they’re regularly followed by men in cars and on the streets while they walk home, to school or the store. They’ve witnessed shootings and lost loved ones to gunshot wounds. They’ve heard stories of girls their age being killed on the streets and in domestic violence incidents.

“Even if it’s not happening to me specifically, just to know that it is happening makes me feel unsure,” Ken’Niyia said.

In addition to not feeling safe, several of the girls said they felt left behind, or that the rest of the city was judging them. “It feels like anything that happens to us, Black women in Los Angeles, is our fault,” said Dalila, 17.

There have been several shootings outside Dalila’s home, including one two years ago, when her cousin was shot in the mouth. The cousin survived.

All of these girls live in the areas that have long seen an outsized share of the city’s violence and systemic neglect, where people live on meager incomes and access to grocery stores and thriving business corridors are scant.

Living here puts girls like Dalila at a higher risk of violence compared to their peers of other races and income brackets. And when they are harmed, Dalila said, they don’t get the same compassion white women do.

“People say, ‘She lived in South Central. She’s a product of her environment,’” she said.

The workshops the girls attended were organized by the Women’s Leadership Project (WLP), a nonprofit that offers mentorship to teen girls and queer youth and educates local high-schoolers on gender-based violence and the social issues that contribute to it.

Though the organization was founded 15 years before Tioni’s death, her short life has galvanized the group, said its director, Sikivu Hutchinson. “I don’t like to say [Tioni’s] a symbol, but she is unfortunately representative of so many things. It’s really just symptomatic of the lack of protection, lack of harm reduction, and the lack of prevention and care,” Hutchinson said.

WLP has been pressuring local officials to focus on the violence Black women and girls face in their schools, homes and neighborhoods. The group is calling for the creation of a youth center in Tioni’s name that would give young people in South Central a safe place to hang out, do homework, and take classes.

“In South Central, we see boarded-up buildings, vacant lots, pot shops and liquor stores, but no youth spaces. All of that is a symptom of the disinvestment in the so-called inner city,” Hutchinson said. “We want all of those resources and services in our community because of the high rates of harm and victimization that young people are experiencing.”

The city of Los Angeles and its police department have touted a strong decline in overall homicides in recent years, but domestic violence killings, which overwhelmingly claim the lives of women, have remained a persistent issue. In 2022, LA recorded 392 homicides, according to LAPD’s annual homicide report, but by 2024 that number had declined to 284. The number of domestic killings remained consistent, though, with 32 murders in 2022 and 33 in 2024. Black women are disproportionately the victims of domestic homicides. Black women make up about 13.5% of the city’s female population, but a third of its female domestic homicide victims.

This trend also extends to the rest of the county. Black women had the highest homicide rate of any racial group in 2024, according to California department of health data. The only other demographics with high rates are Black and Latino men, who historically have made up most of the region’s homicide victims.

It’s not just LA. Black women across the US have long had a higher risk of being killed than women of other races, according to a 2024 analysis of homicide data by the Violence policy center. That year about 700 Black women and about 1500 white women were killed by men. Black women make up 13% of the US female population, white women make up 55%. Black women were most often killed with a gun, by a man they knew.

The city of LA says it’s working to address the high rates of violence by bolstering its response network for domestic violence victims, and by funding programs that can prevent gun violence in the neighborhoods where Black women and girls die most frequently.

The office of the mayor, Karen Bass, pointed to investments the city has made in its nearly 20-year-old gang reduction and youth development (GRYD) program, which operates programs throughout the city, including South Central. Though GRYD is mostly geared toward pulling Black and Latino men and teens out of the cycle of violence, staff also refers families to supportive programs. The program has helped bring down homicides in the city’s hardest-hit neighborhoods throughout South Central by almost 30% in 2025, the mayor’s office said.

California has tried to address the issue at a state level, when in 2023 lawmakers created the Ebony Alert, a first-in-the-nation emergency notification system specifically geared towards finding missing Black women and girls. Since the alert became law in 2024, it has been activated for 182 people. Of those, 175 have been found alive, one was found deceased, according to California highway patrol data.

Still, the racial and gender disparities in victims of violence remain.

Some cities and states have come up with frameworks to address the issue with more fervor. Minnesota created a taskforce made up of elected officials, nonprofit leaders and representatives from law enforcement agencies to specifically look into the killings and disappearances of Black women and girls. The group advises the state’s department of public safety on ways to reduce violence against them, and how to work with service providers to give tailored support to Black victims’ families and domestic violence survivors.

The Minnesota taskforce was in part created in memory of Brittany Clardy, an 18-year-old who was murdered in 2013. Clardy’s family reported her missing after she left to go to a nearby store but then stopped answering calls and texts. She was found dead in her car two weeks later.

The man who ultimately pleaded guilty to her murder was also convicted of murdering another woman, 24-year-old Klaressa Cook, who was found dead in the trunk of a car just months after Clardy.

In the years following Clardy’s killing, her sister, Lakeisha Lee, spoke in front of the state legislature and started a foundation to help support girls who are at risk of being sex-trafficked.

It’s not uncommon for these kinds of efforts to be spurred by people who’ve lost a mother, daughter or sister to violence, said Dr Brittany Lewis, founder and CEO of Research in Action.

“This happens because families endure going to committee hearings to convince people that the death of their family member matters,” she said. “And that what they need is much bigger than the band-aid solutions we’re producing.”

Not only do Black women and girls face disproportionate rates of violence, but when they’re killed, their cases are less likely to be solved. In 2022, the Los Angeles police department solved all killings of Black female victims. But the next year, that rate declined to 90%. In 2024, it plummeted to 67% and in 2025, at a time when the number of homicides in the city was plummeting, just half of the killings of Black women and girls were solved, according to the LAPD’s annual homicide reports.

Shalissa Collier, whose daughter Mikeona Johnson was found dead in the trunk of her car in Los Angeles in September 2020, was determined to beat this trend.

After Mikeona’s death, Collier learned that she had long been abused by a former partner and that her daughter had filed for three separate restraining orders against the man.

Collier says she brought these findings to Los Angeles police, but six months later they came to her home to tell her that the department didn’t have any leads and would be closing the case, Collier said. “LAPD pissed me off. I can’t even sugarcoat it,” she recalled.

Collier began organizing candlelight vigils and press conferences in front of the LA county’s district attorney’s office. She also spoke with independent journalists and on the podcast Misogynoir Murders, which highlights the stories of missing and murdered Black women.

In February 2024, the roommate of Johnson and her partner, Phillip Charles Howze, went to police with new information, and Howze was arrested. He was convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to 15 years to life.

With her daughter’s killer sentenced, Collier in October was finally ready to bury her daughter’s ashes, and she held a burial ceremony.

“I felt like it would be fitting to do it, especially after he got his time. Now she can finally rest,” Collier said.

Misogynoir Murders started out as an attempt to center the stories of Black women and girls in the true-crime genre. Now, host Ronnetta Rideout says she sees it as a community service for the families that want to keep the stories of their daughters, sisters and mothers alive.

“[Black women] were still very underrepresented even in stories, even though we’re overrepresented in the actual data,” Rideout said.

LAPD declined to respond to questions about its initial decision to close Mikeona Johnson’s case. When asked about the department’s approach to solving the homicides of Black women and girls specifically, public information officer Jeff Lee said LAPD “takes all acts of violence seriously, and every homicide is thoroughly investigated. Detectives follow all available leads and work to identify those responsible, leaving no stone unturned in the pursuit of justice.”

He did not offer specifics on whether or not the recommendations from the 2023 city report have been implemented within the department.

California highway patrol said it is still actively investigating Tioni Theus’s murder.

Since her young cousin was killed, Kincy has learned more about the ways vulnerable teen girls are groomed and trafficked in the city’s sex work corridor. According to Mayor Bass, this type of exploitation is a “child welfare crisis”, and she is working with county officials to crack down on it while supporting teen girls and young women who are getting out of the life.

“These are girls and children, not women. This is a child welfare crisis, and I am working with LA county leadership to address it,” she said in a statement to the Guardian. “At the same time, we are holding the people who prey on these children accountable.”

And while Tioni’s family awaits answers from law enforcement, they say members of the South Los Angeles community, too, have a role in preventing violence against Black women and girls, whether it’s reporting underage girls on sex-trafficking corridors to police or supportive services, calling out predators who are grooming teens online, or sharing information that can lead to an arrest.

“I feel like as a community we can’t be silent any more,” Kincy echoed. “We can’t wait for politicians, lawmakers or even the police. We have to stand up and make people accountable.”

Michael Dolphin, Tioni’s great-uncle, agreed. “This is not a white folks problem, it’s not an LAPD problem, it’s not a Mayor [Karen] Bass problem. It’s a community problem, because someone knows what happened,” he said.

He wants the city to pour resources into programs that can rehabilitate young people who have been repeatedly arrested or are currently incarcerated. These investments, he hopes, can stop teen boys from becoming violent.

“We need to figure out ways to catch these kids earlier,” he said. “We need to figure out how to get involved sooner and provide alternatives to hanging out on the street.”

Dolphin remembers his niece as a smart, loving teenager. He saw her often in the mornings, on her way to school, when she would come by to visit her great-grandmother, whom Dolphin was caring for. They would share breakfast and go over her homework together. “She liked her schoolwork,” he said. “And big mama’s house was a quiet, peaceful refuge for her.”

Kincy says she hopes that the story of her bubbly, sometimes clumsy teen cousin who walked on her tiptoes can lead to greater awareness around the increased risk of violence and exploitation Black teen girls and young women face and shed light on stories that received less news coverage than Tioni’s.

“When Tioni’s story hit, it resonated with people because it happened to their kid as well and they didn’t get the exposure,” Kincy said. “We can bring light to these stories through her.”

This article was updated on 11 November 2026 to include a statement from Karen Bass, the Los Angeles mayor.

#215. With $720M round, Britain’s Fractile gets a leg up in the race for AI chips

Fractile, a British startup developing AI chips, has raised a $720 million Series C backed by Britain’s Sovereign AI Fund with hopes of “ensuring the U.K. has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy,” its government stated.

Alongside the likes of Axelera, Etched, and OLIX, this makes Fractile one of the top-funded startup players in the race for purpose-built AI chips. Such chips are one of several avenues being explored to reduce the cost of inference — aka using increasingly demanding AI models in production.

However, Fractile seeks to go beyond hardware with a full-stack approach that also includes a machine learning compiler to maximize the speed at which LLMs will get executed on its chips.

As a result, the company frames itself as a frontier AI company, and its latest round led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Redpoint was priced accordingly. According to the British government, the valuation was “over £5 billion” — quite possibly $7 billion, a figure reported both by the Financial Times and a Reuters source.

Still, Fractile’s main differentiator will arguably be its hardware design. After a pivot, its approach now revolves on DRAM, the most common type of RAM, but stacked on top of each chip in such a way that it is hoping will bypass the usual tradeoff between memory and capacity.

This tradeoff has become more problematic with the rise of agentic AI, as companies seek to perform longer chains of tasks with large models without compromising on speed. As compute struggles to keep up, hopes are high for AI chips, despite their limited availability to date.

In a LinkedIn post, Fractile CEO Walter Goodwin wrote that “there is still a lot of work ahead” for the company, and that the new funding will enable the startup to “ship [its] first chips and systems next year.”

#213. Democrat Scott Colom unseats Cindy Hyde-Smith in shocking Mississippi Senate win

Colom takes victory by razor-thin margin in state that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982

Democrat Scott Colom defeated Cindy Hyde-Smith, the incumbent Republican senator, to become the first Black senator in Mississippi elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.

Colom opened up a narrow lead over Hyde-Smith late on election night. His lead widened as election officials counted absentee and provisional ballots. The Associated Press called the contest on Wednesday, after it was clear Hyde-Smith was not able to close the gap.

“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said in a two-minute concession video, shared on social media. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982. It’s been much longer – not since 1875 – that the state sent a Black senator to Washington. Colom is also the first Black man popularly elected to the Senate in the state’s history – during Reconstruction, senators were chosen by state lawmakers.

With Colom’s election, Mississippi, the first state to send Black lawmakers to Congress, has sent more Black people to the Senate than any other state besides Illinois. Blanche K Bruce, the last Black man elected to the Senate from Mississippi, was born into slavery; John C Stennis, the last Democrat to be sent from Mississippi, was, for most of his career, a staunch segregationist.

Colom’s election capped a national wave of anger at Donald Trump’s administration, sweeping away Republicans in places where Democrats hadn’t been competitive in decades. With the addition of Colom, Democrats will hold at least 55 seats in the Senate – the party’s largest midterm gain since 1986.

Across the south, voters were further motivated by the president’s attempt to drastically redraw Black majority districts, attempting to dilute the largely Democratic voting blocs.

Colom has a track record of success in the state. In 2015, Colom unseated a nearly 30-year incumbent when he was elected the first Black district attorney for the 16th circuit. As district attorney, he had a 94% success rate for convictions. He’s a seventh-generation Mississippian, whose father was a longtime Republican who campaigned for Ronald Reagan and was friendly with Thad Cochran, a longtime state politician who resigned from his US Senate seat in 2018 due to declining health.

A string of Democratic stars visited the state late in the race as the polls showed a tightening race – Cory Booker, Pete Buttigieg, Kamala Harris and Bill Clinton all made appearances for Colom. Trump rallied for Hyde-Smith last month.

Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a federal judge in the northern district of Mississippi. With support from both Republicans and Democrats, he appeared to be on track to a lifetime appointment on the federal bench, when Hyde-Smith blocked him from having a confirmation hearing.

“I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being a US senator,” Hyde-Smith said in remarks to supporters on election day.

In the days after the election, as Colom’s vote-margin inched higher, he kept a dizzying campaign pace, visiting Millsaps College, his alma mater, and local colleges Jackson State University and Tougaloo College. With national and international cameras on him, Colom stopped by small, local businesses, including Marshall’s Music and Book Store and OffBeat, both of which are Black-owned, and Brent’s Drugs, a Jackson classic.

Colom campaigned on the promise that “Mississippi matters”. He told voters that he would represent all Mississippians, even those who supported his opponent – and the president.

A week before the vote, he attended Trump’s rally for Hyde-Smith in Corinth to engage the president’s supporters and listen to their economic concerns. He posed for photos with some rally-goers, as they talked to him about high gas prices, grocery bills and health insurance. He later said the face-to-face conversations helped him convert the unlikeliest of voters to his campaign.

Colom drew national attention for a viral ad that played on his opponent’s response to a question about the rising cost of beef: “You have so many proteins to choose from,” Hyde-Smith told a local television host during the interview. Colom’s campaign seized on the moment, producing a 30-second ad that jumps from her reply to a man grilling beef patties. “Pick another protein?” the man says. “Shiiiit. I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Colom drove a “pick your protein” taco truck around the state, handing out free tacos to voters.

As the days-long counting process commenced, both Hyde-Smith and Colom projected confidence that they would prevail.

National voting groups and attorneys descended upon the Magnolia state, joining the local groups that worked to mobilize voters. Democratic and Republican groups, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) and Democratic election attorneys from the Elias Law Group, have deployed hundreds of volunteers and lawyers to all the state’s 82 counties to oversee the final rounds of counting.

Mississippi has no automatic recount law. A recount can only happen if ordered by a court in response to a lawsuit against a county or county election commission from a political party or campaign. Mississippi law does not establish a system for challenging ballots on a statewide scale, so the process would have to be on a county-by-county basis.

“I assure you,” Hyde-Smith said on election night, “I will continue to be your US senator.”

Asked about those comments at a press conference the next day, Colom replied: “Bless her heart.”

#211. CoreWeave turns to customer prepayments, shorter contracts to fund AI growth

CoreWeave is rewriting how it pays for the AI boom, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings, reported on Tuesday. CoreWeave, a neocloud that rents out the computing power behind AI, said it’s increasingly asking customers to pay up front, borrowing against specific contracts, and even pursuing short-term deals that could lead to higher prices.

The new strategies could help CoreWeave finance its growth more efficiently while squeezing more cash from existing infrastructure. But these bets only hold if today’s demand and pricing power continue.

CoreWeave reported $3.66 billion in revenue, up 168% from the year prior, but it also posted a $709 million net loss and $846 million in quarterly interest expense.

“We will not use the unsecured debt market to fund our business at current yields, nor do we need to,” CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said during Tuesday’s earnings call.

Instead, CoreWeave’s plan is to rely on loans backed by specific customer contracts, drawing on funds as needed to finance most of infrastructure it still has to build to deliver on its significant backlog of $132.5 billion.

CoreWeave also said it expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months, including more than $3 billion tied to signing new customer contracts for capacity it has already built, which requires no additional spending on hardware.

Rivals Nebius and IREN have also relied on hefty Microsoft prepayments to pay for computing capacity, signaling that the industry is moving toward asking Big Tech to pay up for their buildouts.

Upfront payments could alleviate CoreWeave’s immediate borrowing needs, but they also commit the company to providing services at a price that might be less attractive down the road if compute demand continues to surge.

CoreWeave is also looking to capitalize on that growing demand by signing more shorter-term contracts that can command much higher prices.

The company raised prices across its offerings by about 25% in July and by another 10% later in the quarter. Prices are still climbing this quarter, in a way that “more than offset[s] cost increases,” said Intrator.

“We are also allocating more capacity to short-term opportunities, where the pricing justifies it, selling capacity at more than $40 million per megawatt annually, while pricing for new infrastructure on four and five-year contracts is moving to $20 million to $25 million per megawatt,” the chief executive said.

CoreWeave’s financing strategy now revolves around those opportunities. In August, the company closed a $2.6 billion loan, its first designed specifically for shorter-term customer contracts. Known as DDTL 5.5, it lets CoreWeave borrow in installments as it needs the money.

While short-term deals let CoreWeave charge higher prices and change them more frequently, it’s a tradeoff. Lenders give more weight to longer-term contracts, even if they’re priced lower, because they value predictable cash flow and consistency to repay the loan above all.

Even though Wall Street reacted positively to CoreWeave’s earnings, bond investors are much less sanguine. Last month, yields on some of the company’s bonds hit above 15%, highlighting that investors are concerned about the debt needed to fund data center buildouts before those investments see a return.

In short, CoreWeave is finding new ways to expand without relying on unsecured debt. The strategy it has chosen could boost profits, but it also carries greater risk around contract renewals and pricing — and it just goes to show how dependent the AI infrastructure boom is on sustained, and as yet unproven, demand.

TechCrunch has reached out to CoreWeave for more information about its loan facility.

#210. Democrats push to rein in Trump on immigration after voter backlash to ICE raids

Members of Congress seek to ‘bring sanity’ to system but decline to give details on plans to reform or abolish agency

A group of congressional Democrats on Wednesday pushed for immediate efforts to rein in the Trump administration’s sweeping immigration enforcement operation and “bring sanity” to an immigration system that Donald Trump said, after his party’s midterm drubbing, had been “too tough” in certain aspects.

Just over a week after the midterm elections in which the US president’s harsh crackdown on immigration fueled a voter backlash against Republicans, some sitting and newly elected Democrats gathered outside the US Capitol in Washington to advocate for a bipartisan approach to reforms – even as they gear up to take control of both legislative chambers next year.

“I have very aspirational dreams and hopes for immigration reform. But I am also a pragmatist. And as we have – as we continue to have – Donald Trump in the White House, and without a supermajority in the Senate, we need Republican support. So any comprehensive immigration reform must be bipartisan,” said congresswoman Veronica Escobar, a Democrat from Texas whose district includes El Paso on the US-Mexico border.

The group’s press conference included progressive as well as moderate Democrats from the Senate and House, in a show of unity. Many attendees held signs saying “legal pathways for long-term immigrants”.

The one Republican lawmaker slated to attend, congresswoman Maria Salazar of Florida, who has taken jabs at the president over immigration that are rare from his side of the aisle, did not appear.

“There is time still this session for a deal,” said US senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona. “We should try to work, even if we can’t get something this session, next session for a deal. We owe it to this country. We owe it to our friends.”

He added: “Republicans have been saying we will have immigration reform as soon as we have a safe, secure border. We have that right now. We did the job. Now let’s figure out how to right-size our immigration issue. Let’s figure out how to keep families together.”

The remarks followed Trump’s aggressive mass deportation campaign and ruthless moves that dramatically slowed crossings at the border, beginning as soon as he re-entered the White House in January 2025. His Democratic predecessor Joe Biden saw significantly elevated levels of migration at the border, and despite his at times harsh approach, the subject of migration became a high-risk political topic for Democrats, who gained a reputation as being too soft on the issue.

Since then, Trump’s second term has also seen US citizens and immigrants killed by immigration enforcement agents, record numbers of people held in often squalid detention conditions and highly visible, violent tactics in the country’s interior that led many voters to sour on some of his policies or at least how they are carried out.

The president’s mixed messages post-midterms included a tentative offer to make a deal with Democrats to help longstanding and law-abiding undocumented immigrants in the US avoid his crackdown. But that contrasted sharply with his actions so far, and shortly after the comments were recorded for TV he named Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff despite him being the architect and orchestrator of Trump’s most draconian, white nationalist immigration policies.

Trump has also signaled that he intends to use his presidential veto power often to block Democratic-supported legislation if it passes Congress.

At the same time, experts expect a barrage of investigations and oversight hearings from Democrats next year in an effort to bring accountability.

But lawmakers on Wednesday said they did not want to wait that long to begin improving the immigration system, highlighting two existing bipartisan bills they believe could be a practical starting point. There was no detailed talk on Wednesday of how to abolish or even significantly reform Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) despite it being a hot topic during the election campaign.

The first highlighted by the lawmakers who spoke on Wednesday, the American Dream and Promise Act, focuses on providing legal pathways to a green card for undocumented immigrants brought stateside as children, colloquially known as “Dreamers”, as well as people with temporary protections to remain in the US while their country of origin experiences serious turmoil.

Not only has Trump not offered such a path, his administration stopped recognizing many temporary legal statuses awarded under past Democratic administrations and has been deporting or trying to deport many who have papers or long-term legal options.

Lawmakers on Wednesday pitched the proposed legislation as an opportunity to act even before the new Democratically-controlled Congress is sworn in come January, asking for Trump’s help in getting it past the finish line.

“We all can agree that the immigration system is broken. But we can start today on a path to build a foundation with the Dream and Promise Act, and to move forward next year when we take over to make even more reforms,” said representative Sylvia Garcia of Texas.

Separately, the Dignity Act is the only bipartisan, comprehensive immigration reform bill introduced in over a decade, with 35 Democratic and 20 Republican sponsors. It couples strict border security measures with some protections for undocumented people.

Salazar is the bill’s lead sponsor. But Escobar, one of the Dignity Act’s fiercest champions and its co-author, said that she and her colleagues planned to reshape it over the next few weeks before reintroducing it next legislative session.

“If we can get this passed this upcoming Congress, we can do even more in 2028 to grow and expand what we can do for immigrants, immigrant families, and our economy and our communities,” she said. “We need to bring sanity back to the immigration system. We can do this. We will do this.”

Meanwhile, representative Henry Cuellar, another Texas border-area Democrat, expects to chair the House appropriations homeland security subcommittee in the new year – and thus control the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) funding.

He said he has a list of guardrails to revert ICE, which comes under the DHS agency, to its role prior to Trump’s second term.

#209. Israeli military veterans, a backbone of protest movement, vow to keep demonstrating

In a sea of Israeli flags, Yiftach Golov holds one that looks a little different.

Among the hundreds of thousands of protesters who took to the streets for the 13th week in a row on Saturday, Golov hoists a brown flag that represents a group called “Brother and Sisters in Arms.”

They are veterans – many, like Golov, from elite forces – who now feel they are fighting on a new battlefield: To save Israeli democracy.

“We believe this is our responsibility to go once again called to the flag of the nation to stop this madness to defend Israel,” Golov said, as he weaved his way through the protesters on Tel Aviv’s Kaplan street, between the high-rises that house many of Israel’s high tech companies.

During the second intifada, in the early 2000s, Golov served in a special forces reconnaissance unit. He was never before particularly political, focusing more on getting his PhD in biophysics from Tel Aviv University.

But when the protest movement against the Israeli government’s judicial overhaul plan began in January, Golov attended one a demonstration and soon became one of thousands of veterans, and now military reservists, who have taken up the cause as their new mission.

Some, including elite Air Force reservists, have taken it a step further, threatening not to heed the call to train or even serve in protest of the government’s plans planned judicial changes, which would give the governing parties more control over Israel’s judiciary.

Others have taken to becoming some of the most active organizers and demonstrators. Last week, a group from Brothers and Sisters in Arms protested by carrying a figure wrapped in the Israeli flag on a stretcher, the way they would carry a wounded comrade off the field.

While Golov says he has not taken the drastic step to refuse service, he understands the motivation.

“We’re fighting for justice and liberty, just like the American story, that’s the values that that are being represented symbolized back when we look at our flag, that’s something that was lacking lacking for the last few decades. So basically, we reclaim the flag,” he said.

Palestinian taxi driver recounts surviving attack by right-wing protesters

Fellow members of the group, all wearing brown shirts with the organization’s logo, come up and say hello. They’re sprinkled all throughout the protests. One is even leading the “Pink Front,” a group of coordinated drummers who look like they are dressed for a rave, and often lead the chants at the protests.

They’re using skills they learned in the military – how to organize, how to mobilize – now for the protests. But more importantly, they say they have the same type of motivation.

“The very deep feeling that you are part of something bigger than yourself, that (you’re) allowed to sacrifice anything that is needed, whether it’s your career, health, seriously mental health,” Golov said. “We all have a mission, you’re willing to do it at any cost. You’re very determined, you know that you are on the right side, you’re carrying the torch of light. That keeps us being highly motivated despite the fact that we’re not sleeping for days.”

Israel’s protest movement is made up of many disparate groups, but the pressure from Israel’s much vaunted veterans has been seen as a key to moving the needle.

Last Monday, after weeks of sustained protests and the largest general strike in Israeli history, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a pause to the legislation, to allow time for negotiations with the opposition.

But despite the announcements, protesters are still out in the streets in large numbers. CNN affiliate Channel 12 in Israel estimated the size of Saturday’s demonstration in Tel Aviv at about 150,000 people. Organizers claimed it was 230,000.

Last week’s mass protests and widespread strike action came after Netanyahu said he had decided to fire Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for advocating a delay in passing the legislation – a move that Netanyahu has since delayed, sources told CNN, due to “the present security situation.”

In his televised speech calling for a delay, Gallant had said the pause in the legislation was needed “for the security of Israel,” citing the refusal of some Israel Defense Forces reservists to train in protest of the government plans. He said pressing ahead with the proposals could threaten Israel’s security.

Under pressure at home and from allies abroad, Netanyahu said he would delay votes on the remaining legislation until after the Knesset’s Passover recess in April “to give time for a real chance for a real debate.”

“Out of the responsibility to the nation, I decided to delay … the vote, in order to give time for discussion,” he added.

But Netanyahu indicated that the delay was only temporary. He insisted that the overhaul was necessary, and reiterated criticism of refusal to train or serve in the military in protest at the planned changes. “Refusing is the end of our country,” he said.

Many protesters don’t believe that the pause is real, or say it’s simply a stalling tactic to give Netanyahu some breathing room and get the protesters to go home before he plows on with the reforms.

“We will start doing deactivation only when we will know 100% that Israel state will stay a functional democratic country. Whatever needs to be done for that,” Golov said.

#207. Olaf Sakkers is betting he can beat the emerging-manager squeeze

Entering into the world of venture capital has never been easy, especially as a first-time fund manager. But it’s especially daunting right now.

According to PitchBook data, firms raising their fourth fund “or later” captured a whopping 88.2% of U.S. VC fundraising dollars through the first three quarters of this year, while first-time funds captured a measly 4.5%. Just 81 first-time funds closed in the first nine months of 2026. That puts the year on track to be the worst for first-time managers in at least a decade, according to PitchBook’s estimate.

Olaf Sakkers has spent the past five years proving that difficult doesn’t mean impossible. He founded his firm RedBlue Capital in 2021 and closed its first fund with roughly $5 million in capital commitments in 2023. He has now held a first close on a second fund that he says will total at least $50 million.

Raised in South Africa, he studied anthropology at Princeton, focusing on global health and health policy, and wrote his thesis on HIV in his home country. He moved to Israel after graduating and was drafted into the Israel Defense Forces, where he says he had a desk job liaising with the U.S. military, and where he became interested in autonomous vehicles.

An introduction led to Michael Granoff, founder of the venture firm Maniv Mobility and an early backer of electric-vehicle startup Better Place. Granoff, who had money to invest, hired him on the spot, Sakkers says. Neither had been a venture investor at that point, so they built a fund “almost by accident,” learning as they went. Sakkers says he ran the investment process day to day, backing Israeli founders who were bringing cybersecurity skills into the automotive world, and later expanding to the U.S. and other markets.

By 2021, Sakkers says, he was an equal partner in Maniv’s economics, but he wanted something different — more formal and scalable — so struck out on his own. Today, RedBlue backs what he calls the “real economy,” including robotics, logistics, manufacturing and energy.

Getting to this point has been a test of endurance as much as salesmanship, seemingly. Sakkers says that institutional limited partners, outfits like endowments and pension funds, have been the toughest to win over because his checks are small (and theirs are comparatively huge) but also because their risk model is built to “avoid getting a zero,” which is why they tend to gravitate toward established brands.

Says Sakkers, it’s akin to founders who come to be seen as “inevitable,” after they’ve previously founded another company. Meanwhile first-time founders often battle against the “gravity of perception,” meaning a more dominant brand can bend how people perceive a newer one.

His answer has been to let the results speak, but it takes time. “It’s a long-term game of building trust, demonstrating performance over time,” Sakkers says.

The first fund was a proof of concept, backed by LPs he had known for a while, including family offices. The second draws on family offices and institutions.

RedBlue writes small checks, $50,000 to $100,000, mostly joining deals led by other investors rather than leading them. That lets it do more deals and be “the last investor that they take” on by promising practical help, including introductions to lead investors like Andreessen Horowitz and Thrive Capital, and to customers. Founders expect little from VCs, in Sakker’s view, so RedBlue tries to overdeliver on the support part.

By his account, the results are strong. Of 28 investments, he says that 15 have been marked up, and he cites a net internal rate of return of “significantly above 50%.” There has been just one exit — an acqui-hire — so most gains from the tiny fund remain on paper and unrealized.

Public records support part of Sakker’s story. HappyRobot, which RedBlue backed early, raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.2 billion valuation in August. Westmag, which makes motors for drones and robots and which Sakkers backed at pre-seed alongside Nat Friedman, emerged in June with an $11 million seed led by Andreessen Horowitz. Flai, an AI startup for car dealerships, followed its 2025 seed with a $27 million Series A. And Humble Robotics, a driverless-truck startup in whose $24 million seed round RedBlue participated, announced a $51 million Series A led by Obvious Ventures earlier this month.

Sakkers argues that discipline is his edge. RedBlue publishes thesis essays, such as one on robotics, and runs on a custom database that he built with Claude Code to log relationships, meeting notes and introductions.

That lets him and his lone full-time principal, based in New York, work asynchronously. AI agents, he says, are “useless if they just have to guess,” so everything gets written down. He contrasts that with Benchmark’s more artisanal model, which he says suits a firm with a record he lacks. Long exit timelines for physical-world companies don’t worry him, either: even a $50 million to $100 million fund, he says, can sell stakes on the secondary market.

The data isn’t uniformly grim. Smaller venture capital funds between $1 million and $10 million consistently outperform larger funds of $100 million or more at the top end of net TVPI (total value to paid-in capital, which compares a fund’s total value to the money invested in it) across recent vintages tracked by the software outfit Carta.

In the meantime, Sakkers is out there knocking on doors, making introductions between disparate parties, and calling up reporters like this one to tell his story. It’s not easy to make a mark in a world where the spoils accrue to the few, but he says he never seriously considered a safer job. “Life is short, and regrets last forever,” he says.

#205. UK Privy Council overrules Trinidad and Tobago gay sex law

A London court has overturned a Trinidad and Tobago law criminalizing consensual sexual relations between male same-sex couples. As a result of the colonial legacy, it is the independent country's last court of appeal.

A man from Trinidad and Tobago has won a legal appeal lasting almost a decade in the last court of appeal available to him — the judicial committee of the Privy Council in former colonial power Britain.

Jason Jones, a gay man born in Trinidad and Tobago, had challenged the Caribbean nation's Sexual Offences Act outlawing consensusal sex between adult males, saying that it breached his fundamental rights under the country's constitution.

He initially won his case at Trinidad and Tobago's High Court, but the government and religious organizations managed to partially overturn the ruling once more, prompting Jones to the take the case to the island nation's highest appellate authority — the Privy Council in  the UK.

"To discriminate against somebody simply because of who they choose to love is simply ridiculous," Jones told the Associated Press after Tuesday's judgment was rendered.

The Privy Council in London is the final court of appeal for some Commonwealth countries including Trinidad and Tobago, although that issue was already contentious in some circles prior to Tuesday's ruling.

A panel of five judges unanimously allowed Jones' appeal, dismissing a counter-appeal from the Caribbean country's Attorney General.

It found that two sections of the country's Sexual Offenses Act 1986, criminalizing "buggery" and "serious indecency" respectively among same-sex couples, violated Jones' fundamental rights to private and family life set out in the 1976 constitution.

The court wrote in its ruling that "the rights and interests of Mr Jones which are at stake involve a particularly important facet of his existence and identity since the ability to form an intimate and loving relationship with another person lies at the core of the right to private and family life."

The anti-gay laws that call for up to five years in prison have not been enforced in recent history, but critics say they still send an intimidating message.

Judge Philip Sales said as he announced the ruling that "the current understanding of the fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life is that it protects such a core part of human identity as one's sexual orientation."

Sales added that "laws which seek to criminalize such activities cannot be justified."

Trinidadian authorities argued that because the 1986 laws were passed with a super-majority and constituted criminal penalties that dated back to colonial times, prior to the constitution, they could be considered "existing law" and override the individual constitutional rights in certain circumstances.

But the Privy Council judges found that the so-called "proviso" for this special status — "unless the Act is shown not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual" — had not been met.

One of Jones' lawyers, Anand Ramlogan, is a former attorney general of Trinidad and Tobago and argued against this position earlier in the case.

"Constitutional rights exist precisely because majorities are not always right," Ramlogan said. "They ensure that the dignity and equality of every citizen are not left to the changing tides of public opinion."

Jason Jones is a 61-year-old born in Trinidad and Tobago.

Openly gay since the age of 16, he said he fled the country in 1996 because of homophobic violence and discrimination.

Speaking to the Associated Press on Tuesday after what he termed a "stunning victory," he said he would describe himself as a "very angry gay man," whose anger had helped him persist in his legal appeal for so many years.

"Society has treated me worse than a criminal," he said. "There is a real sense of vindication with this judgment. Finally, the courts are seeing that they need to step up because our politicians are so toothless."

He said he became inspired to speak out after losing friends to HIV/AIDS and after meeting American singer-songwriter Nina Simone when she toured the island nation for three weeks in 1984, when he was 19.

"Nina was the one who said, 'Jason, get off this rock and go see the world,'" he said, calling it a defining and life-changing experience.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trinidad and Tobago's government, the country's Council of Evangelical Churches and its largest Hindu organization, Sanatan Dharm Maha Sabha, contested the case, which has wound its way through several courts since the appeal was launched in 2017.

In 2018, Trinidad's High Court found the laws unconstitutional. But in 2025, a local appeals court partially reversed the ruling. Trinidad's Court of Appeals subsequently allowed Jones to seek a ruling from the final appeals court in England.

The case was being closely watched by activists across the Caribbean, with similar laws in place in several other countries in the region.

The Bahamas decriminalized homosexuality in 1991.

The UK repealed laws in overseas territories Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands in 2001.

Judges in Barbados, Dominica, St. Lucia and Antigua and Barbuda have also recently struck down similar laws.

But in former British colonies Grenada, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago and St. Vincent and the Grenadines it remains a crime.

The UK only decriminalized gay sex in 1967, more than four centuries after the so-called "buggery" laws were first introduced under King Henry VII, and more than a century after the last executions for the crime. People still faced prosecution or the threat of it for consensual adult gay sex until after World War II, with surely the most famous later-years case being that of computing and codebreaking pioneer and war hero Alan Turing.

Democrat Scott Colom wins race for US Senate in Mississippi

How Colom won deep-red Mississippi with little help from Democrats

The Associated Press now projects that Democrat Scott Colom has been elected to the US Senate to represent Mississippi, defeating the Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The AP made the call after Colom’s lead expanded to 4,669 votes on Wednesday.

Colom will be Mississippi’s first Black senator since 1881, when Blanche Kelso Bruce, who was born into slavery, served during the post-civil war Reconstruction era. In 1874, Bruce was elected by Mississippi’s state legislature to serve in the US Senate, a seat he held from 1875 to 1881.

Colom, a local prosecutor, waged a savvy campaign to take advantage of Donald Trump’s deep unpopularity, making a viral campaign ad that focused on the high price of beef and even talking to Trump supporters waiting on line before a rally the president held for Hyde-Smith in Mississippi the week before the election.

After Hyde-Smith appeared on stage with Trump, Colom’s campaign posted video of her praising the unpopular president with the theme music from Curb Your Enthusiasm added to the clip.

In a video statement posted on social media on Wednesday, the Mississippi Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith acknowledged that she has lost her seat to Democrat Scott Colom.

“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

The ad is simple, less than half a minute long, but many say it was the moment the nation took notice of Mississippi’s US Senate race.

In it, the incumbent Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a cattle farmer, answers a reporter’s question about the rising price of beef: “You know, you have so many proteins to choose from,” she says.

The ad then cuts to a man flipping burgers on a grill. “Pick another protein?” he says. “Shhiiiiii – I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

The viral ad was for Hyde-Smith’s Democratic challenger, Scott Colom, who won the Senate seat on Wednesday, becoming the first Democratic senator in Mississippi since 1982 and its first Black senator since the Reconstruction era. His ads were relevant to Mississippians and created memorable slogans – an early ad highlighted the history and progress of the state, while a more recent one spoofed the hit film Sinners, filmed in Mississippi. But his efforts to engage Mississippians didn’t start there.

Colom spent the past year reaching Mississippi residents where they were. From driving a “pick another protein” truck that offered free tacos, to talking to students and alums at college homecomings, to chatting with voters queued to see Donald Trump, Colom campaigned on an idea that’s not novel to Mississippians, but one that the rest of the country is only starting to fully realize: “Mississippi Matters.”

And he did it with little help from the Democratic party.

#198. How AI worsens online violence against Middle East women

Women in the Middle East already have to deal with an above-average share of online harassment and violence. The proliferation of AI-enabled tools is making it worse.

It happens all the time, says Kholoud al-Ameri, an Iraqi journalist and the editor of a news website.

"Female journalists here are often getting messages, and mostly from men," she explains. "They somehow find you online and then they say they just want to talk or they want to add you on Instagram or Facebook," says al-Ameri, who also heads a network of female journalists working on climate change stories. "Sometimes it's hard because the men say they're our readers and we don't want to discourage them. But I usually tell the women just to block these guys."

Syrian activist Yaman Amer tells of similar experiences as a result of writing about women's rights online — she says she gets hundreds of critical comments. "When I talk about women's rights online in a patriarchal society, that's just how things are," Amer, who is studying to be a lawyer in Damascus, told DW. "Not that I accept it. Out of every thousand offensive comments, there's usually one or two that make me feel like I have to report them because they're particularly vile. As in, they're extremely vulgar or threatening. And then it's more than just harassment. It's on a whole other level, humiliating and degrading."

Online harassment of women isn't unusual anywhere. Studies by a variety of organizations show that somewhere between 40% and 60% of all women worldwide have experienced it, while 65% have witnessed it.

There is no single standard for assessing the level of online harassment because surveys often use different types of questions or research methods. But in general, women around the Middle East appear to be dealing with a higher-than-global-average level of what is known as "technology facilitated gender-based violence," or TFGBV.

The United Nations Population Fund defines TFGBV as a harmful act "that is committed, assisted, aggravated or amplified ... by the use of information communication technologies," or other digital tools, "against a person on the basis of their gender."

According to research by UN Women, the UN body dedicated to gender equality, 68% of women in the Middle East have had to deal with it, while almost all — close to 100% — have seen it online.

In a 2025 study, UN Women found that 49% of women using the internet in the Middle East don't feel safe from online harassment. The number goes up to almost 70% if the women are more publicly visible activists, journalists or politicians.

And it is already clear that the increased availability of artificial intelligence-powered applications is making online harassment worse.

AI has the potential to supercharge this kind of abuse, the UN Women briefing points out, "both by facilitating the spread of targeted disinformation as well as the proliferation of image-based abuse and deepfake pornographic videos."

Of the women who had experienced online violence while working, around a quarter had already identified "abuse that was generated or amplified by AI tools," the briefing said.

The potential for using the latest technology in order to harass people online has always been there, says Siddharth Venkataramakrishnan, an analyst at the London-based Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD), which investigates extremism. "But it's just become easier to produce harmful content at scale and in a hyper-targeted way. And the production of non-consensual imagery is a real marker of the democratization of that technology, so it's moving away from primarily targeting celebrities to just regular people."

Venkataramakrishnan has been researching incidents that occurred at the beginning of 2026 when Grok, the AI-powered chatbot belonging to Elon Musk's company SpaceXAI, became able to alter photographs to depict a fully dressed subject as nearly naked. The scandal caused Grok's services to be restricted but, as Venkataramakrishnan pointed out, safeguards across different AI models tend to be inconsistent and users can still find work-arounds to get similar results.

In conservative cultures in the Middle East, the threat of this kind of half-naked picture of a woman being published has serious real-life implications, mostly because of what is and isn't acceptable for women around the region.

What makes the increase in AI-generated fakes even more problematic in the Middle East is that online abuse also has a higher chance of having offline effects.

"Norms related to honor, family reputation and male control can turn digital abuse into real-world consequences," a June briefing by the World Bank notes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

It's also often not easy for people targeted with this kind of abuse to find legal protection or even somewhere to report it. While some Middle Eastern countries have cybercrime laws, most don't specifically address gender-based online violence nor have they been updated to grapple with AI-related abuse.

Last year's UN Women survey found that 36% of women said they were just told to ignore the online violence, while 23% were blamed for it themselves and 12% were subjected to physical punishment by their families because of it.

Other studies indicate that only about 7% of women who experienced technology-facilitated violence later report it to law enforcement. Various concerns stop them from doing so, including having to present sexualized images or answer personal questions in front of strangers — often also anathema to many women in the region.

The women who had experienced online harassment said they would often just block the perpetrators and around a quarter said they then became more careful about what they posted online. Twenty percent deleted their accounts or left social media altogether.

The rapid growth in AI-enabled harassment can also be more problematic in the Middle East because of the situations the women targeted find themselves living in.

Displacement, war, conflict and instability can all make women more vulnerable to online abuse and exploitation. Even the rapid development of AI-related technologies in a country without corresponding legal guardrails or digital literacy can increase the risk.

For example, observers point out that Saudi Arabia, a generally conservative country with strict rules for female behavior, is going through an accelerated program of digital transformation.

And in Syria, after the ousting of the dictatorial Assad regime, many Syrians "rushed into social media to speak freely," journalist Zaina Erhaim wrote for the Arab Reform Initiative in July this year.

Previously. digital polices had been closely policed by Syria's dictator and a political post could see the writer thrown in jail. But now Syrians "are navigating this newfound liberty without guardrails, oversight or protection," Erhaim argues, and female activists are paying a high price for it, especially where "gender intersects with sect."

In a policy paper published in May, the Syrian Women's Political Movement explained just how bad online abuse had become. In focus groups with 120 women from all around Syria, the majority of participants agreed that digital abuse had become a way of shutting them up. Younger activists reported personal pictures were being stolen from social media, then used against them.

"Smear campaigns targeting women's 'honor' and systemic defamation are actively deployed as punitive measures against any women who attempt to express a critical political opinion," the organization wrote, arguing that what was needed was a law that criminalized digital violence.

If you or someone you know have experienced any kind of gender-based violence, the website lila.help (https://lila.help) lists trustworthy helplines and NGOs that offer support in almost every country around the world.

#197. Burnham raised safety concerns about Manchester ‘monster’ warehouse, inquiry hears

PM wrote to transport commissioner to oppose ‘megashed’ in Astley shortly before he entered No 10

Andy Burnham raised safety concerns about dozens of lorries leaving a “monster” warehouse near a primary school because there was “no safe crossing” for children, a public inquiry has heard.

Concerns about the 18-metre-high “megashed” in the village of Astley, Greater Manchester, are being examined by Britain’s office of the transport commissioner.

A deputy transport commissioner, John Baker, launched an environmental public inquiry after significant local opposition to the round-the-clock operation by the logistics company Whistl.

Whistl is asking for a licence to increase its number of HGVs at the site from 40 to 50 and the number of trailers from 60 to 70.

But people living nearby told the inquiry on Wednesday that granting the licence would worsen the “catastrophic” impact on those living nearby, with some left suffering with anxiety, sleep deprivation and depression.

The inquiry also heard that shortly before he became prime minister, Burnham wrote to the transport commissioner’s office to oppose Whistl’s plans.

In the letter sent in February, which was not shown at the inquiry but has been seen by the Guardian, the then Greater Manchester mayor expressed concerns about the route taken by dozens of HGVs to access the 17-acre site near his Makerfield constituency.

Burnham said schoolchildren would be forced to share the road with huge lorries “despite there being no pedestrian crossings, no lollipop service, no traffic calming and sections where the pavement is extremely narrow or ends entirely”.

John Peters, who co-founded the Astley Warehouse Action Group, told the inquiry, at the Brick Community stadium in Wigan, that it was a recipe for disaster, adding: “I hope I never have to say I told you so.”

The Whistl warehouse, which was named Britain’s joint-worst new building this year, was approved by Wigan council in 2024 after a planning application by PLP, a firm part-owned by Peel Group, one of Britain’s biggest landowners which is run by the billionaire John Whittaker.

The outcome of the inquiry, expected in early December, is seen as a test case of how local groups could challenge similar large industrial developments across Britain.

The Labour government has relaxed planning rules to allow big logistics projects on previously protected land as the UK strives to compete in the race for AI and the growing e-commerce market, which increasingly relies on next-day deliveries.

Peters, who said he had lived in the village since 1979, was in tears as he likened Whistl’s “megashed” opening in the summer to “a plane crash-landing in that field”.

He said one year ago the only medication he took was a single statin to lower blood cholesterol levels: “I now take high blood pressure [medication], statin, anti-depression and a sleeper. That’s the state I’m in. I know in our group we’re in a truly bad state so I dread to think what would happen [if Whistl’s licence was approved].”

David Gerrard, a builder who lives opposite the site, appeared emotional as he described the effect on his wife and their three daughters.

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

He said they were routinely woken throughout the night by the sound and light from lorries. Gerrard, whose house has declined in value by an estimated £170,000 as a result of the disruption, said he recently counted 113 wagons over a seven-hour period from 5.30am. “How are we supposed to live with this? It’s ruining our lives,” he said.

James Healey, a leading acoustics expert commissioned by the residents, said he had never before seen planning approval given to such a noisy warehouse so close to people’s homes.

He said: “In my 22 years in consultancy I’ve never seen a planning application be approved with a sound impact such as this, so it’s unprecedented in my experience.”

A report by Healey, who chairs the UK Institute of Acoustics building acoustics group, concluded that those living closest to the site faced “severe health risks” from the excessive noise.

Carole Retford, whose property is overshadowed by the warehouse, became close to tears as she described being “exhausted through lack of sleep” and mood swings from “anxious to quite depressed”.

Another resident, Paul Bullow, said: “Physically, mentally, it’s draining, it’s constant. It never stops. It just brings levels of stress that weren’t there before but are now there all the time. It’s completely unacceptable.”

In September, Whistl volunteered to pause overnight operations between midnight and 6am and introduced quieter electric vehicles. Giving evidence, Whistl executives conceded that they might not have chosen the site had they known the level of concern it would cause.

Patrick Sadd, Whistl’s barrister, said the company accepted the “extremely moving” evidence and that the impact on some residents had been “far-reaching”. He said the company deserved credit for working “tirelessly” to find a solution and would continue to do so, including exploring the possibility of erecting sound-insulating structures.

#194. A new approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine shows early promise

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

China and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

The US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

As long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, says study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

The immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler said.

Mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with new variants.

The new nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

The researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

“You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler said.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

As promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans

“They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, said Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the new research.

The study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an update.

It also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler says they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss company called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

Other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland said. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a new vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

In reality, Poland said, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

“That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he said.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax says it may not survive

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a company called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team says it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very important in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler said.

They have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

FluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Sign up here to get The Results Are In with Dr. Sanjay Gupta every Tuesday from the CNN Health team.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

Another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler said, so it would have to be used carefully.

#192. British soldier charged with rape of army servicewoman in Cyprus

L/Cpl Nicholas Horne, from 4th Battalion of Royal Regiment of Scotland, charged with one count of rape on 23 October

A British soldier has been charged with the alleged rape of a UK army servicewoman in Cyprus.

L/Cpl Nicholas Horne, who serves in the 4th Battalion of the Royal Regiment of Scotland, also known as The Highlanders, was charged with one count of rape on 23 October, the Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC) said.

He was arrested on 19 October, two days after the DSCC was informed of the reported rape of a woman serving in British Forces Cyprus.

Horne was remanded in custody pending a court-martial hearing.

The charge comes after an investigation of the DSCC’s major crime team, conducted with service police partners.

A British army spokesperson said: “We can confirm that L/Cpl Nicholas Horne was charged with one count of rape on 23 October 2026, following an investigation by the Defence Serious Crime Command.

“We recognise the great courage it takes to come forward and report an offence. Anyone convicted of a sexual offence will be discharged from the service”

The DSCC, which investigates serious crime committed by military personnel, said anyone affected by sexual offences in the armed forces is encouraged to contact them.

The Ministry of Defence has stepped up efforts to tackle sexual violence and sexual misconduct in recent years.

Last year it announced specialist teams would be deployed at UK military locations in the UK and overseas. The move came after the MoD’s first official survey of sexual harassment across the armed forces found nearly one in 10 women serving full-time in the British military had been subjected to an assault or other non-consensual sexual activity in the previous year.

#189. India: CPCB addresses stark Delhi pollution data gap on Diwali night
